nameStory: Herb Robert gets its name from Saint Robert of Molesme, an 11th-century French monk who founded the Cistercian order and was known for his healing work with herbs. This little geranium has a long history in folk medicine, earning it the honor of bearing the saint's name. Some say the 'Robert' might also come from the Old French 'herbe à Robert' meaning 'bright red herb,' referring to its reddish stems and autumn foliage.
description: Herb Robert is a delicate annual wildflower that looks almost fern-like with its deeply divided, lacy leaves. This small member of the geranium family typically grows 6-18 inches tall with thin, often reddish stems that branch out in a sprawling pattern. Its tiny pink flowers have five petals and bloom from spring through fall, followed by distinctive beak-like seed pods that give all cranesbills their name. The entire plant often takes on reddish tints, especially in fall or when stressed.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply cut, fern-like leaves divided into 3-5 segments, each further lobed. Feel soft and slightly sticky to the touch, with a strong, somewhat unpleasant smell when crushed - often described as 'foxy' or musty.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink flowers about 1/2 inch across with five rounded petals and prominent white or pale pink stripes. Flowers appear in pairs on thin stalks and have 10 stamens with orange anthers.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thin, brittle stems that are often bright red or reddish, especially at the joints (nodes). The reddish color becomes more pronounced in fall or when the plant is growing in sunny, dry conditions.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Long, pointed seed pods that look like a crane's beak, about 3/4 inch long. When ripe, they split dramatically and fling seeds several feet away with an audible 'pop' if you touch them gently.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing and sprawling, forming loose mats or growing as scattered individuals. Often found growing in small colonies, with plants having a somewhat disheveled, delicate appearance.

habitat: Herb Robert thrives in shady to partially shady spots with moist, rich soil - look for it in woodland edges, rocky areas, and along stone walls. It's equally at home in disturbed areas like gardens, roadsides, and waste places, and can even grow on shingle beaches and limestone outcrops. This adaptable plant often appears where soil has been recently disturbed or in the gaps between rocks and pavement.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges early with fresh green, lacy foliage and the first small pink flowers begin appearing in late spring. Plants are at their most vibrant green before summer heat sets in.
seasonality.summer: Continues blooming steadily through summer with flowers and developing seed pods often present simultaneously. Stems may start showing reddish coloration, especially in sunny or dry locations.
seasonality.fall: Plants take on beautiful reddish-purple tones throughout, with leaves, stems, and even flower stalks turning crimson. Seeds are actively dispersing with a satisfying 'pop' when ripe pods are touched.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, but seeds that dispersed in fall will be ready to germinate the following spring in suitable locations.

funFact: Herb Robert's seed pods are like tiny biological catapults - when ripe, they explosively split and launch seeds up to 20 feet away at speeds that would make a baseball pitcher jealous, all triggered by the slightest touch or change in humidity!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small crane's-bills, but Herb Robert's strong 'foxy' smell when crushed is a dead giveaway - no other local geranium smells quite so pungent. Remember: if it stinks, it's probably Herb Robert!
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this wild geranium with the colorful potted geraniums sold at garden centers - those are actually pelargoniums from South Africa. True geraniums like Herb Robert are much more modest in appearance but are the original geraniums that gave the whole family its name.
compareHints: Among New England's wild geraniums, Herb Robert is the most delicate and lacy-looking, with much more finely divided leaves than the larger Wild Geranium. While Wild Geranium has bold, palmately-lobed leaves and grows in clumps, Herb Robert's leaves look almost fern-like and the plant has a more sprawling, weedy growth habit. The strong smell when crushed also sets it apart from all its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild geranium stands out from its cranesbill cousins by its substantial size, soft pink flowers, and preference for rich woodlands.
Among New England's crane's-bills, bloody crane's-bill stands out for its deeply divided leaves that are cut almost to the base, creating very narrow segments.
Among New England's crane's-bills, rock crane's-bill is unique for its low, mat-forming growth and intensely fragrant leaves - most others grow more upright and have much less scented foliage.
Northern cranesbill is much smaller and more delicate than wild geranium, with tiny lavender flowers instead of large pink ones.
Thunberg's Geranium is much smaller and more delicate than our common Wild Geranium, with more finely divided leaves and smaller flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Carolina crane's-bill has the smallest flowers - much tinier than the showy inch-wide blooms of wild geranium or the medium-sized flowers of Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, meadow crane's-bill is one of the largest and most robust, forming much bigger clumps than most relatives.

Among New England's crane's-bills, dusky crane's-bill is unique for its nearly black flowers with backward-curved petals - our native wild geranium has pink flowers that face upward, while Herb Robert has small bright pink flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, dove's-foot stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety leaf texture and low, mat-forming growth habit.
Among New England's crane's-bills, this is one of the tiniest and most easily overlooked.
Purple-vein geranium stands out from other New England geraniums primarily by its bright blue flowers - most other species have pink, white, or purple blooms.

Among New England's crane's-bills, cut-leaved crane's-bill stands out for having the most finely divided leaves - while wild geranium has broader, less deeply cut leaves and Herb Robert has more triangular leaf segments, cut-leaved crane's-bill looks almost feathery.
Among New England's crane's-bills, little-robin is the tiniest - much smaller than wild geranium or Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Long-stalked stands out for its exceptionally long flower stalks and deeply dissected leaves.

Richardson's geranium differs from New England's common wild geranium by having paler flowers with more prominent dark veining, perfectly straight (not curved) seed beaks, and more finely divided leaf segments.
Wood crane's-bill differs from our native wild geranium by having more deeply dissected leaves and typically stronger purple coloring with more prominent petal veining.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Siberian Crane's-bill would be one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
